html:
The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom, founded in London in 1694 to lend money to the government. It became the model for central banks around the world.

It was created in the middle of a costly war against Louis XIV's France. A group of investors lent King William III £1.2 million at 8 percent, and in return they were made a company with the right to take deposits and issue notes. The idea came from a Scot, William Paterson. Parliament stood behind the debt, which made lenders trust it.

How its role grew:

  • It managed the government's debt and became its main banker.
  • Its notes became the most trusted paper money in the country; from 1844 it gradually gained a monopoly of note issue in England and Wales.
  • It held the country's gold reserve and set its lending rate, and under the gold standard of the 1800s that rate steered credit across the world.
  • It learned to act as lender of last resort, lending freely to sound banks in a panic, a rule set out by Walter Bagehot in 1873.

Cheap, reliable government borrowing let Britain pay for its long wars with France in the 1700s and helped make London the centre of world finance. The Dutch had shown the way, and Sweden's Riksbank (1668) is older, but the Bank of England became the pattern others copied.

It was nationalised in 1946 and given independence to set interest rates in 1997.
sum: The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom, founded in London in 1694 to lend money to the government. It became the model for central banks around the world.
